title: Baking Moon Dirt Into Breathable Air
kidSummary: Moon dirt isn't like garden soil—it is crushed gray rock full of trapped oxygen! With enough heat and electricity, astronauts can bake oxygen straight out of lunar dirt.
scienceDetail: NASA's lunar surface technology work develops oxygen extraction from regolith, including molten regolith electrolysis and carbothermal reduction. Regolith is roughly 40–45% oxygen by mass, bound in silicate and oxide minerals like ilmenite.

title: Why Astronauts Stack Moon Dirt on Their Roof
kidSummary: Earth has a giant invisible magnetic bubble and thick air that block Sun storms. The Moon has neither! Stacking thick walls of moon dirt acts like armor against space radiation.
scienceDetail: NASA DONKI tracks coronal mass ejections and solar particle events (protons above 10 MeV). On the Moon there is no magnetosphere or thick atmosphere, which is why Silica Station crews stack moon dirt and shelter during a flare.

title: Why Batteries Matter When the Sun Sets
kidSummary: A single night on the Moon lasts about two whole Earth weeks, and temperatures drop colder than any freezer! Solar panels make zero power in the dark, so crews must charge batteries early.
scienceDetail: One lunar synodic day lasts about 29.5 Earth days, with roughly 14.7 days of sunlight and 14.7 days of darkness. In Silica Station, the dark period is simplified to 5 rounds (Rounds 5–9) for classroom play.

title: Moon Dust Sticks Like Static Cling
kidSummary: Lunar dust is sharp like tiny glass shards and carries static electricity, so it sticks to spacesuits and solar panels—blocking sunlight until astronauts clean them.
scienceDetail: Apollo crews found that lunar dust clogged mechanisms, interfered with instruments, coated radiators and abraded spacesuits. NASA studies dust mitigation because the dust is fine, abrasive and electrostatically charged.
nasaSourceName: NASA Dust: An Out-of-This World Problem

title: Frozen Water Hiding in Dark Craters
kidSummary: Deep craters near the Moon's South Pole never see sunlight. They hold ancient frozen ice that rovers can mine and split into drinking water and air!
scienceDetail: NASA's LCROSS and LRO missions confirmed water ice deposits inside permanently shadowed regions near the lunar poles, which is why Artemis targets the south polar region for a base camp.
nasaSourceName: NASA Water Ice on the Moon

title: Why Moon Astronauts Never Skip Exercise
kidSummary: On the Moon you weigh six times less than on Earth! That sounds fun, but without daily workouts, astronauts' bones and muscles shrink fast.
scienceDetail: NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) collects spaceflight studies showing that microgravity causes bone mineral loss and muscle atrophy unless crews exercise and eat well.

title: Measuring Real Astronaut Radiation in Space
kidSummary: Invisible cosmic rays hit astronauts faster than on Earth! Radiation sensors aboard the Space Station measure exact dose rates every minute so engineers know how much armor crews need.
scienceDetail: NASA OSDR's RadLab portal publishes real absorbed dose rate readings (microgray per hour) from ISS instruments such as DosTel detectors. The dose changes as the station passes through different radiation zones, which is why thick shielding matters.

title: Growing Fresh Food on the Moon & in Remote Communities
kidSummary: Rockets can't bring fresh salad every week! Astronauts grow leafy greens, berries, and veggies inside energy-saving Moon greenhouses—and the same tech helps Northern towns on Earth grow food all winter.
scienceDetail: The Canadian Space Agency (CSA) studies how crews eat and grow food in space, including closed-loop greenhouse ideas that recycle water, save electricity and could serve remote Northern communities on Earth.

title: Space STEM Activities for Kids Ages 7–12
kidSummary: Want to try real space experiments at school or home? The Canadian Space Agency shares free hands-on games, coding challenges, and moon-farming activities for young explorers.
scienceDetail: The CSA's youth and educator resources provide bilingual activities for classrooms, libraries, camps and clubs, connecting space exploration with nutrition, robotics and sustainability on Earth.
nasaSourceName: CSA · Resources for youth and educators
